title: James Webb Space Telescope optics, explained by NASA

chunks.text: the most prominent and beautiful part of nasa's james webb space telescope is its gold primary mirror with a smaller secondary mirror suspended out in front the webb telescope is a reflecting telescope technically an astigmatic telescope this means that its concave primary mirror captures the light and reflects it to the secondary convex mirror which reflects the light back to the concave rectangular-shaped tertiary mirror and then finally to the flat fine steering mirror which sends the light through a hole through the center of the primary mirror to focus on the science instruments behind the primary mirror this kind of telescope enables a wider field of view and minimizes optical distortion the primary and secondary mirror form what is called a casa grain telescope similar to the hubble space telescope it's this third powered mirror that makes web and astigmatic telescope webb has the largest primary mirror ever

How big is Webb's primary mirror, and wh.text:
The James Webb Space Telescope's primary mirror is 21 feet and 3 inches (6.5 meters) across [2]. 

It must be segmented and folded for launch because its size is larger than the fairing of the rocket used to transport it into space [2].

Why were the mirrors made the “wrong” sh.text: The mirrors were manufactured to the "wrong" prescription at room temperature so that they would achieve the "precisely the right shape" once they reached their operating temperature of -388 degrees Fahrenheit (-233 degrees Celsius) [3]. This is necessary because beryllium, the material used for the mirrors, changes its shape with temperature and only becomes stable at very cold temperatures [3].

How do engineers align the mirrors once.text:
Once the James Webb Space Telescope is in space, engineers align the mirrors using the following process:

*   **Wavefront Sensing and Control:** Engineers on the ground use Webb’s near-infrared camera and a process called "wavefront sensing and control" to align the mirrors [1].
*   **Actuator System:** Behind each of the 18 mirror segments is an actuator system that allows engineers to move each segment precisely in every direction and slightly modify its shape [3].
*   **Ongoing Maintenance:** The mirrors are retuned as needed throughout the mission to maintain their alignment [1].
